Saudi Arabia Imposes Sweeping Import Tariffs, Disrupting Trade and Industry

RIYADH, June 11 — Saudi Arabia has imposed broad import tariffs on a wide array of goods in a move government officials say is aimed at supporting domestic industries and improving the kingdom’s trade balance. The new tariffs, which took effect late Monday, have already disrupted supply chains and raised concerns among businesses across multiple sectors.

The Ministry of Commerce said in a statement that tariffs ranging from 10% to 25% now apply to items including machinery, vehicles, chemicals, and consumer electronics. Food products and raw materials for essential industries remain exempt for the time being, but analysts warn that higher costs for imported parts and equipment could affect production and investment decisions throughout the economy.

Saudi Arabian Oil Co is among the companies contending with the new measures, as it relies on imported machinery and technology for facility maintenance and upgrades. A company spokesperson declined to comment on the immediate impact but said the situation was being “closely monitored.”

“The policy is part of Vision 2030’s goal to diversify and strengthen local manufacturing,” said Deputy Minister of Industry Fahad al-Mutlaq on Tuesday. “We recognize there will be short-term adjustments, but we expect this to boost employment and encourage investment in Saudi businesses.”

Importers and trade groups voiced concerns about the abrupt rollout. “Our members are facing delays at customs and uncertainty over pricing,” said Maha al-Dosari, chairwoman of the Saudi Importers Forum. “We urge the government to provide clearer guidance and transitional support.”

Logistics hubs in Jeddah and Dammam reported congestion as importers scrambled to clear shipments before the higher tariffs took effect. Retailers said they anticipate price increases on imported electronics and appliances, while manufacturers warned of possible production slowdowns if key components become scarce or more expensive.

Economists estimate the tariffs could affect more than $30 billion worth of annual imports. “It’s too early to judge the long-term benefits,” said Riyadh-based analyst Omar al-Sayegh, “but the short-term disruption is real and significant for both businesses and consumers.”
